[...] there remains a second fundamental difficulty: solving the number-theoretic problem of ruling out the existence of an enormously long non-trivial cycle of the 3x + 1 function. title: The Collatz conjecture, Littlewood-Offord theory, and powers of 2 and 3
quote: Suppose the weak Collatz conjecture is true. Then for any natural numbers a, k with 2^a > 3^k, one has [2^a − 3^k ≥ (1+ε)^k for an absolute ε > 0 (Proposition 7)] [...] Thus we see that any proposed proof of the Collatz conjecture must either use transcendence theory, or introduce new techniques that are powerful enough to create exponential separation between powers of 2 and powers of 3. Unfortunately, once one uses the transcendence theory bound (7), the size q of the cyclic group Z/qZ becomes larger than the volume of any cube in S, and Littlewood-Offord techniques are no longer of much use (they can be used to show that S is highly equidistributed in Z/qZ, but this does not directly give any way to prevent S from containing 0).
hook: F4 (meta-statement: no-cycle proof => exponential separation), F3

It shows that infinitely many k have at least k^{1−ε} distinct such cycles of period at most log k, and infinitely many k have no such cycles having period length less than k^{1/3}.
